Alexander III of Macedon

Alexander III of Macedon (20/21 July 356 BC – 10/11 June 323 BC), most
commonly known as Alexander the Great, was a king of the ancient Greek
kingdom of Macedon. He succeeded his father, Philip II, to the throne in
336 BC, at the age of 20, and spent most of his ruling years conducting a
lengthy military campaign throughout Western Asia and Egypt. By the age of
thirty, he had created one of the largest empires in history, stretching
from Greece to northwestern India. He was undefeated in battle and is
widely considered to be one of history's greatest and most successful
military commanders.

== Early life ==

Alexander was born in Pella, the capital of the Kingdom of Macedon, on the
sixth day of the ancient Macedonian month of Hekatombaion, which most
probably corresponds to 20 July 356 BC. His father, Philip II, was king of
Macedon, and his mother, Olympias, was a princess of Epirus. Until the age
of sixteen, Alexander was tutored by the philosopher Aristotle.

== Reign ==

Accession

Alexander became king of Macedon in 336 BC, at the age of 20, following
the assassination of his father Philip II. He began his reign by
eliminating potential rivals to the throne, including his cousin
Amyntas IV.

Balkan campaign

Before crossing to Asia, Alexander secured his northern borders and
suppressed a revolt in Thebes. The Theban revolt was crushed and the city
was destroyed as an example to the rest of Greece.

== Conquest of the Persian Empire ==

In 334 BC, Alexander crossed the Hellespont into Asia with an army of
approximately 48,100 soldiers. He defeated the Persian forces commanded by
the local satraps at the Battle of the Granicus. This victory opened Asia
Minor to Macedonian advance.

The decisive confrontation with King Darius III came at the Battle of
Issus in 333 BC, where Alexander routed the Persian army and captured the
king's family.

== Death and legacy ==

Alexander died in the palace of Nebuchadnezzar II, in Babylon, on 10 or 11
June 323 BC, at the age of 32. He had planned further campaigns, including
an invasion of Arabia, but no successor arrangement was in place. His
empire fragmented among his generals in the wars of the Diadochi.

Some historians note that Alexander never lost a battle; others caution
that ancient sources are uneven and that later accounts embellished his
reign. The city of Alexandria in Egypt, founded by Alexander in 331 BC,
became a major center of Hellenistic learning.
